title: We rejected 98% of the ideas our AI trading agent generated
author: Rare_Inflation3178
selftext:
Not because they were bad.

Because they couldn't survive validation.

Some failed execution assumptions.

Some only worked in one regime.

Some disappeared after realistic slippage.

Some fell apart with tiny parameter changes.

Honestly, generating ideas isn't the bottleneck anymore.

Validation is.

Curious if anyone else building AI trading systems has found the same thing.

comments.author: DarkandBoring
comments.body: without feeding it the proper data its just going to randomly create strategies, so Yes i had the same problem at first, then i started scouring for data, and meanwhile forward testing slowly and surely strategies started getting promoted.

replies.author: Rare_Inflation3178
replies.body: Totally agree. The good data sources and  data cleaning is very important. Did you find anything interesting when you do forward testing compare to backtesting?

comments.author: Good_Character_20
comments.body: Same experience here, and honestly the 98% getting killed is the system working, not a problem. The part that took me longer to accept is that a high kill rate doesn't protect you by itself. If you run enough ideas through the same validation gauntlet, a few survive on luck alone, and those are the dangerous ones because they show up wearing a clean bill of health. The more you generate, the more the validator itself becomes the thing that's overfit. What helped was keeping a final holdout the generator never sees and only checking it once, on the handful that already passed everything else. Thins the survivors even further, but the ones left are the ones I actually trust.

replies.author: Rare_Inflation3178
replies.body: That’s a really interesting perspective. It’s also why I’ve been adding things like PBO and deflated Sharpe. The more strategies you generate, the easier it is to fool yourself unless every stage of the validation pipeline is treated as another potential source of overfitting

comments.author: LankyAwareness2258
comments.body: Same experience building on the algo side — regime shift and slippage are the two silent killers. A strategy can post a gorgeous in-sample curve and still die the moment you swap "filled at the print" for a realistic fill model, or the second the volatility regime changes underneath it. What's worked for me is treating walk-forward validation across at least two regimes as a hard gate before anything gets near live capital — if it can't survive that, the backtest numbers don't mean much. Curious what your rejection criteria actually weight most — execution assumptions or regime robustness?

replies.author: Rare_Inflation3178
replies.body: I weight execution first. If realistic fills and costs kill the edge, regime robustness doesn’t matter much. If it survives execution but only works in one regime, I’d classify it as a conditional strategy instead of throwing it away. I’m increasingly treating the whole process like a gated pipeline, where each stage is trying to kill the strategy for a different reason before it reaches live capital.
